clinicalPearls: A rare rigid flatfoot deformity in which the talus is fixed in a near-vertical position and the navicular is irreversibly dislocated dorsally onto the talar neck
The classic appearance is a rocker-bottom foot with a convex plantar surface, a prominent talar head medially in the sole, and the forefoot dorsiflexed and everted
The deformity is rigid and cannot be passively corrected, which is the crucial distinction from a flexible calcaneovalgus or positional flatfoot
About half of cases are associated with neuromuscular disease, chromosomal abnormalities, or syndromes such as arthrogryposis, so a broader examination is essential
Lateral radiographs taken in maximal plantarflexion show the talus remaining vertical and failing to align with the first metatarsal, confirming the fixed dislocation
Modern management favours a reverse-Ponseti (Dobbs) serial-casting technique to stretch the dorsolateral soft tissues, usually followed by minimally invasive surgery to reduce the talonavicular joint
Untreated, the foot becomes painful and functionally disabling with callosity over the prominent talar head and difficulty with shoe wear
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital vertical talus is a fixed dorsal dislocation of the navicular on the talus, locking the talus into a vertical, plantarflexed orientation while the calcaneus is held in equinus and valgus. Contracture of the dorsolateral soft tissues, including the tibialis anterior, extensor tendons, and the peroneals, together with a tight Achilles tendon, maintains the deformity, and the head of the talus is forced plantar-medially to create the convex sole. The condition may be an isolated idiopathic malformation but is frequently a manifestation of an underlying neuromuscular imbalance or genetic syndrome, and abnormalities of the HOXD10 gene have been described in some familial idiopathic cases.
additionalDifferentials: Flexible calcaneovalgus foot, which is supple and positional
Oblique talus, a milder reducible variant intermediate between normal and vertical talus
Flexible flatfoot with a supple, correctable arch
Tarsal coalition presenting as a rigid flatfoot in older children
Congenital talipes equinovarus at the opposite end of the deformity spectrum
Paralytic or neuromuscular flatfoot from cerebral palsy or myelomeningocele
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing or simulated weight-bearing anteroposterior and lateral foot radiographs
Forced plantarflexion lateral radiograph to confirm the irreducible talonavicular dislocation
Forced dorsiflexion lateral view to demonstrate fixed hindfoot equinus
Assessment for associated neuromuscular disease including a full neurological examination
Genetic evaluation and karyotype where a syndrome or chromosomal disorder is suspected
Spinal imaging when a neural-tube or cord anomaly is considered
redFlags: A truly rigid rocker-bottom foot that resists all passive correction
Features of arthrogryposis, a chromosomal disorder, or another syndrome
Signs of an underlying neuromuscular condition or spinal dysraphism
Bilateral deformity with a positive family history suggesting a genetic cause
Progressive callosity, pain, or skin breakdown over the plantar talar prominence
reference.prognosis: With early serial casting and appropriately timed surgery a plantigrade, functional foot can usually be achieved, though results are less predictable in syndromic or neuromuscular cases; late or untreated deformity leads to a painful, stiff, poorly shod foot.
pitfalls: Mislabelling the rigid deformity as a benign flexible flatfoot and delaying treatment
Omitting the forced plantarflexion radiograph, which is needed to distinguish vertical from oblique talus
Failing to screen for associated neuromuscular disease or genetic syndromes
Attempting correction with casting alone and expecting full reduction without surgery
Underestimating the likelihood of recurrence and the need for prolonged follow-up
references: Dobbs MB et al., idiopathic congenital vertical talus reviews
management: Begin treatment with the reverse-Ponseti (Dobbs) serial-casting technique to progressively stretch the contracted dorsolateral soft tissues
Follow casting with minimally invasive surgery — talonavicular joint reduction and pinning with percutaneous Achilles tenotomy — to correct the fixed dislocation
Maintain correction with post-operative bracing and orthotic support to prevent recurrence
Evaluate for and manage an underlying neuromuscular disorder, chromosomal abnormality or syndrome such as arthrogryposis, as roughly half of cases are non-idiopathic
Obtain spinal imaging where a neural-tube or spinal cord anomaly is suspected
Arrange genetic evaluation and counselling for syndromic or familial cases
Manage within a paediatric orthopaedic multidisciplinary team
